segments.text: Right here, halfway through the poem, something weird occurs. My tone shifts in a way I don't remember at all.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: No longer do I see you glancing out beyond our window, wishing yourself other places very far from here. I think you found contentment. I think you found belonging. I think you have found a refuge where safety subdues fear.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Why had my mom given me such hell over this thing? The poem wasn't incendiary, nor was it damning of my mother. If anything, it seemed to wish her well. Here are the last lines.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: Look no more out the window. Look no more through the door. Look not beyond horizon. It's not foreign anymore.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: You found what you've been wanting. Your roots grow deep and true. You found a soul to worship and someone who loves you too.

segments.speaker: Linda Maum
segments.text: OK. The ending was good.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Linda Maum
segments.text: But I will say that at that point, I probably wasn't listening anymore. And that's why I didn't hear the positiveness of it. You no longer have to look. You can go out and be happy with this person that's going to smoke with you. I wasn't going to be alone in this dark age of sin. It's negative to me.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: Still?

segments.speaker: Linda Maum
segments.text: Yeah. Yeah, the beginning is definitely negative still.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: OK, so for me that's painful to hear, because I was really acknowledging how much you were struggling. And to me, that was what I was trying to do with the beginning, was acknowledge everything that you were going through that was so, so hard.

segments.speaker: Linda Maum
segments.text: I could see that. You tell me that, and I can understand it. I'm sorry that I didn't hear the positiveness in it.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: I accept your apology. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Linda Maum
segments.text: [CHUCKLES] [SIGHS] Oh, phew.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: I probably owe my mom an apology as well. I mean, now that I'm rereading it for the first time since the wedding, I get why she was so upset and hurt. It's a pretty dark picture to present of someone on their wedding day. I also get how she couldn't hear the nice things I was saying. Frankly, I didn't remember at all writing the end with that much compassion toward my mom and graciousness toward Mr. X, but hearing it, I do remember feeling that way.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: We were dealing with hard things as a family before my mom got remarried. My brother Brendan had gotten really sick. He basically moved into the Yale New Haven Children's Hospital when he was 10 years old because he was seizing uncontrollably. His heart would stop out of nowhere. It was a terrifying time.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: Mr. X was intolerant of everyone, but he was gentle with my brother, kind. He helped calm my mom down. I know this meant a lot to her and also to Brendan, especially because our father was sort of checked out emotionally from what was going on. I do remember thinking, this is a thing to hold on to here. This is his saving grace.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: I wish I'd made things simpler for my mom back then. I wish I could have said more clearly, I'm worried about you. But anger is the teenage version of worry, and I was very angry. My mom wouldn't tolerate me saying negative things about her partner, so I bottled them inside, which made me snippy and resentful.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: I stopped being nice to my mom. I stopped being light and silly with her. And as it turns out, I had reason to be worried.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: Two days after the wedding, at the age of 49, my mom had a massive stroke. There had been signs she wasn't well on her wedding day already. And in the days following her hospitalization I developed a theory that her body, not her mind, knew that the marriage was a mistake. I ran this by my mom.

segments.speaker: Linda Maum
segments.text: I think that's true. I mean, why was I sweating so much? Why was I-- I think it's true.

segments.speaker: Linda Maum
segments.text: I knew. I knew when I was buying my dress. I knew when I wasn't as happy. I do believe that I anticipated this awfulness ahead of time.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: In your body?

segments.speaker: Linda Maum
segments.text: In every fiber.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: Oh, jeez. I mean, I think to me that's heartbreaking to hear, because that's what I thought was happening.

segments.speaker: Linda Maum
segments.text: Oh, no. I'm just going to start crying.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: That's all right. You can cry, Mom. It's all right.

segments.speaker: Linda Maum
segments.text: OK, I'm crying, so put that in. OK, so I should have called off the wedding. And I knew that, because I was just overwhelmed with everything, end of story.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: I entered this conversation with a bunch of questions from my mother, but it was coming down to one.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: How come you didn't listen to your guts? I think there were a lot of moments where you could have, and you didn't. Were you raised to defer to men, or?

segments.speaker: Linda Maum
segments.text: I was raised that I knew nothing. I mean, I was always wrong.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: You were raised to believe you knew nothing?

segments.speaker: Linda Maum
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: Because you're a woman?

segments.speaker: Linda Maum
segments.text: My mother told me this. So my mother was very domineering. And she made me believe that I was worthless and everything else. And so when I married Mr. X, I think that came back to haunt me, all my negativity against myself. And I think I didn't listen to myself because I couldn't be right. I couldn't be right.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: That's so wild to hear. Because when I was little, my mom was the most capable person-- physically, socially, financially, a total financial whiz, the best dressed, the best looking, the best driver, the most fun, all of these fantastic things. And she had a real reputation still among my friends in school. Yeah, it's emotional to think of. Among my friends in school, it was just like, how everyone looked up to Linda Maum.

segments.speaker: Linda Maum
segments.text: Well, to me this is all very sad. Because, again, it goes back to my mother-- and I hate doing this-- going back to my mother and blaming my mother for some of the things I became.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: And she was a huge smoker, if I'm remembering correctly.

segments.speaker: Linda Maum
segments.text: Oh, giant, giant, giant. I was so angry at myself for being a smoker. I just didn't want to smoke, and then you made it a--

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: So I hit a nerve?

segments.speaker: Linda Maum
segments.text: Yep. Yep.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: My mom also had one main question for me.

segments.speaker: Linda Maum
segments.text: Why did you dislike me so much as a teenager? You kind of have answered that, really, with all the things that were going on.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: But do you want to stop there and let me answer it?

segments.speaker: Linda Maum
segments.text: Sure, if you have-- yeah.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: I have additional--

segments.speaker: Linda Maum
segments.text: [SIGHS]

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: I'm going to bristle at the word "dislike" because I actually liked you a lot, and I looked up to you in a lot of ways. What I could not stand was that you let yourself be walked all over by lesser men, by men specifically, but also men that either didn't seem to deserve you or were actually bad people that weren't respected. You really were such a strong-- you want to say something?

segments.speaker: Linda Maum
segments.text: Yeah, I want to know what men they were. I thought it was just Mr. X. I mean, I don't remember anybody.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: Out of respect for my father-- I'm still grieving. He just passed. I don't want to talk too much about my dad, but my father did not always treat you with a great amount of respect. So I do include him in some of the men that I feel you were subservient to.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: What I saw growing up in Greenwich, Connecticut in the '80s and '90s when Greenwich was truly the bedroom town of Wall Street, what I saw was a lot of vivacious men who got to go somewhere else all day long and come home to children that were bathed and these beautiful women that were their wives-- put out fresh flowers, had dinner out. And the man just came and put his feet under the table, ate the food, and then got to go take a load off in a study. And so growing up, I was like, well, I'll be my dad. I'll be the man. I want to come home and have dinner at the table. I want to drive a cool car to work.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: And so something I bristled against with you is at a certain point, you were taking on so much, and it didn't necessarily seem to be bringing you joy. And Mr. X came into the picture. And in the beginning, I think he did-- he seemed to really worship you. But certainly, as the years went by, I saw a man who demanded to be served and did not fetch as much as his own ice cubes. And that made me really angry at you. I wanted you to stand up for yourself.

segments.speaker: Linda Maum
segments.text: Well, I think it's-- in my mind it was dislike of me because of the way you talked to me and the way you avoided me. I could never see it any other way. Your tone of voice, I mean, I don't know how it could understand that that was because of my lack of respect for myself.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: Yeah. No, I don't think you could have. I mean, I was a B.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: My mom's got a point here. I was sending mixed signals. I loved her. I was mean to her. I wanted her to be a feminist baddie who kicked out Mr. X, but I also benefited from her commitment to homemaking-- the awesome dinners, her driving me around.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It was confusing. I was confusing. But I was clear on one thing, Mom. You chose him over us. You kept on choosing him.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But one night last October, she made a different choice. In the kitchen of the house that Mr. X had designed to look art deco in style, but instead came out looking like a White Castle burger joint, my mom fell and broke her back. Though it was early in the evening, Mr. X was too drunk to help her. She lay on the floor for hours. Finally, he brought her her cell phone so she could call an ambulance herself.

segments.speaker: Linda Maum
segments.text: When I was on that floor, I swore I was going to do everything I could to get rid of him.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: She was hospitalized for months, unable to walk. Before the accident, I'd almost given up on my mom, but now she told me that she'd reached a turning point. She gave me power of attorney to fight in court on her behalf to evict Mr. X.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: For months, I went everywhere with legal paperwork in case I was called into court. It was hard, and it was ugly. It was the hardest thing I've ever done in my life, actually. But we won.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: Mr. X left the house in an unholy state. I spent weeks cleaning up after him, boxing up his possessions. My mom came home from the hospital. My brother and his wife moved in with their cat, who took a particular liking to my mom.

segments.speaker: Linda Maum
segments.text: I didn't know how complicated it was going to be to get about. And at that point, I didn't know you were going to be so instrumental in doing it. Because of the amount of time you spent down here, I realized how much you cared about me. Until then, I really didn't know. I didn't.

segments.speaker: Courtney Maum
segments.text: Mr. X drove us apart, and kicking him out is what brought us back together. It's a strange thing to rally around, but this is where we are. My mom is 79. I'm nearly 50. We have the rest of our lives to catch up on what we've missed.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Courtney Maum. Her latest novel is called Alan Opts Out. Dana Chivvis produced this story.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: We did reach out to Mr. X. And he told us he's designed hundreds of houses. He had lots of friends. He says he never left any house in any kind of disrepair in his life.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Coming up, a man goes back to the job of his teenage dreams to see what is the same and what is gone forever with the passage of time. That's in a minute on Chicago Public Radio when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Today's program, intergenerational space travel, stories of people braving the vast distances that separate young and old, trying to understand life on the other side of the divide. We've arrived at Act Two of our program. Act Two-- Cinema Veri-teen.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So when one of our producers, Ike Sriskandarajah, was a teenager, he had the greatest job he could humanly imagine. And that was, he worked at a movie theater. Wore a cummerbund to work every day, snuck around the managers with secret schemes of his own. This was back in 2003, more than 20 years ago. And Ike wanted to know, is the job still the best? He traveled back to his hometown in Wisconsin and spent some time at his old movie theater, the Marcus Point Cinema in Madison.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: My friend Marc vouched for me to his manager. That's how I got hired there. And Marc knew how to make the most of the job. He taught me which door was the easiest to let your friends in, how to give away free popcorn by filling up discarded plastic bags so you don't mess up your popcorn tub count, and why volunteering to clean the bathroom was actually secretly a great job, because you got out of the concession stand, and you could sneak into a movie for a scene or two on the clock.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: By senior year, I stacked lunch and study hall together in my schedule, and I'd treat friends to a school day matinee with popcorn and soda. I felt like a teen god, second to none in the pantheon of high school jobs, except maybe drug dealer.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: When I got back to my old theater, the outside looked the same-- classic old Hollywood movie marquee, and inside there's still busy, stain-masking carpet and the long tunnel with theaters on either side. It even smelled the same.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: I had asked to speak to teens, employees who were the same age I was when I started, but the company's comms team and their HR department said no. Instead, I could talk to a 26-year-old assistant manager named Darren Klingaman. He was behind the ticket booth when I arrived-- clean shaven, wearing a dress shirt with little flowers and a tie to match. Darren told me he did not apply for the same reasons I did, namely free movies.

segments.speaker: Darren Klingaman
segments.text: No, it was just-- I just lucked out that that was a perk. I didn't know about it until afterwards.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Oh, wow. OK.

segments.speaker: Darren Klingaman
segments.text: It was a nice surprise.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Nice surprise.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Darren was just looking for any job. Besides getting to see movies, what about the other things that made the job so fun back in the early aughts? Are they still part of it? I ran all my favorite hijinks we pulled at the movie theater by Darren.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Before I tell you about the first thing, I just want you to remember our brains were still developing when we thought this was so funny. So basically, if you were the person who ripped tickets, you were supposed to say, enjoy your show. But some genius came up with a twist that involved referencing male genitalia of specific dimensions. I told Darren about this.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: We'd mumble under our breaths, enjoy your chode.

segments.speaker: Darren Klingaman
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: I was wondering if that's still happening.

segments.speaker: Darren Klingaman
segments.text: Not that I'm aware of.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: You've never heard somebody say, enjoy your chode?

segments.speaker: Darren Klingaman
segments.text: No, I have not.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Do you think that joke's funny?

segments.speaker: Darren Klingaman
segments.text: [SIGHS] I mean, I didn't laugh.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: I noticed that.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: In the early aughts, it killed, at least with the kids working at the concession stand.

segments.speaker: Darren Klingaman
segments.text: How many people just said, excuse me?

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: I think that was the most common, because we're mumbling it.

segments.speaker: Darren Klingaman
segments.text: You're mumbling it, right. Yeah, OK. Yeah. I mean, I think it could use some work.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: So that's a change. In 2026, chode's over, folks.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Another thing that I thought was so fun was volunteering to flatten boxes out back. If that sounds boring, you don't know the WrestleMania technique that my friend taught me. Basically, you could fill up the industrial dumpster out back with unflattened boxes, pull yourself up to balance on the metal edge, and then launch yourself into the air and drop the People's Elbow on a box.

segments.speaker: Tom Reichilt
segments.text: Well, I tell you, that sounds like a very interesting workman's comp issue, getting ready.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: That's area general manager Tom Reichilt, who corporate PR asked to join. So many things I loved about this job are gone. We wore tuxedos to work made of this magical material that was impervious to nacho cheese stains. During a tornado, we got evacuated into the manager's office, where we took an ID from the lost and found that looked enough like me to buy malt liquor exactly once.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Now, kids are never let anywhere near the lost and found. The mini donut machine burned me, but it made delicious donuts. Back in the day, it burned Area General Manager Tom Reichilt too.

segments.speaker: Tom Reichilt
segments.text: I probably have one here somewhere, maybe there. A little different these days.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: That's gone too. But what about the big one, my favorite benefit of the job-- letting my friends in for free? It really was the coolest thing I could think of, to be able to grant this wish to anybody-- a free night at the movies, a drink, popcorn. We were allowed to bring in one guest, but I was always happy to let in more friends through the back door near the dumpster. Darren says that, yes, that perk is still around, but these days, the back door is not necessary.

segments.speaker: Tom Reichilt
segments.text: Just have them walk in the front door, come greet them over here, and we'll hook them up. I always let them all know that there's no reason to be sneaky in any way. If you want your friends to come see a movie, tell me, and I'll get them in. I mean, it's a perk.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: So they're allowed to bring in their friends. But calling out to an unscientific survey I did of three teens around America who work in movie theaters right now, I learned they don't want to. One 18-year-old in Kansas City says she prefers watching movies at home, where you can talk to your friends during the show and watch basically any movie ever made. What a waste. Darren at least understands how bringing someone in for free has the power to actually change your life.

segments.speaker: Darren Klingaman
segments.text: When I first started here, a couple months later, I met my girlfriend. I brought her to a date here after hours. That might not technically be allowed.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: What do you mean, after hours?

segments.speaker: Darren Klingaman
segments.text: Oh, everything was closed. We were closed down. I asked her if she wanted to come see a movie. So we watched Wicked.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Whoa, you brought your girlfriend here because you had the keys to the place.

segments.speaker: Darren Klingaman
segments.text: I did. I had the keys. She wasn't actually my girlfriend quite yet. Good first date.

segments.speaker: Darren Klingaman
segments.text: I knew Wicked was one of her favorite musicals. So it was like, perfect thing. Wicked just came out. Why don't we watch it? Private showing and the biggest screen we can.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Darren ushered her into an empty theater. Sat her down in the best seat in the house. Popcorn, Diet Coke in the cup holder. Brought a sweater because theaters get chilly. And then he ran up to the projectionist booth, fast forwarded through the ads, and ran back down to sit with her just in time for the show to start.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: That was two years ago. Now they're engaged. What other job would let you pull off a first date like that?

segments.speaker: Darren Klingaman
segments.text: Honestly, I mean, it was so memorable. We still think about it.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Now, tell me if I'm overstating it, but would you guys be getting married if it wasn't for that?

segments.speaker: Darren Klingaman
segments.text: I would hope so, but I don't know. It's a good question because of how big of a thing it was and how meaningful and unique it was that it definitely bumped me up some points. So hopefully, but definitely not as easily.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: It's really similar to the thing that happened to me.

segments.speaker: Darren Klingaman
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: When I was here--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I told Darren that I also once tried to impress a girl while on the job. When I met her, I filled up a discarded plastic bag with popcorn and slipped it to her. Another time, I let her and her friend in the back. I'm no longer wearing a tuxedo to work, but that girl I snuck in, we're married and have two children. The job today definitely seems less fun, but there's still a little movie magic left.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Ike Sriskandarajah. He's one of the producers of our show. By the way, none of the three teenagers I talked to knew what chode meant, but some of them thought it was funny anyway.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act Three-- Mama, Can You Hair Me? Myra Flynn is in her 40s, and the person across the divide in this story is six. It's her daughter. The two of them have been in a bit of a standoff when it comes to getting ready for school in the morning. It was going so badly, Myra started recording these morning showdowns, trying to figure out if there was some way to fix things. Here she is.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: My mornings used to look so different. In my younger days as a touring musician, I'd greet the sunrise on my way home from a gig in some random city and face plant into my bed. But now I start my day at 7:10 AM, engaged in a battle of wills with my daughter Avalon over her hair.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: Hey, baby. It's time to do your hair. No, we're going to do it because you got to be at school in 10 minutes.

segments.speaker: Avalon
segments.text: But Mommy.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: When I was a kid, my mom and I had a similar hair routine. She would sit me down at the breakfast table every morning, grab a cup of water and a hard bristle brush, and rake through my curls. It hurt like hell, but there was no point in complaining because my mom made it clear we didn't have time for any of that. My hair had to get done. That's just how it was. And that's just how it is for Avalon.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: Black hair is Black hair. And look, I'm not doing box braids or knotless styles, or writing her name in the side of her head with cornrows. I'm just trying to comb through it and put it in a ponytail so that no one looks at us crazy.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: So every morning, I take her hair out of whatever shape it's landed in after a night of sleep without a bonnet. I still haven't found one that stays on her head. Then I grab three different brushes, a big jar of leave-in conditioner, a spray bottle full of water, and get to work, which Avalon, who's six, hates.

segments.speaker: Avalon
segments.text: Ow.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: Stop, baby. Avi, it's not that bad. Stop, stop, stop. No, no. I can't use that brush. I have to use this brush.

segments.speaker: Avalon
segments.text: I just wanted to hold it.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: No, baby. You need to just-- please, can you just look forward, and bend your neck for me. Bend your neck down.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: For the record, holding this brush is a stalling tactic for Avalon. She wants to hold it so I can't use it. And I see straight through you, Avalon Mathis Wills. I know my daughter.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Avalon, by all intents and purposes, seems impervious to pain. I've literally watched her face plant from the top of monkey bars onto the grass, only to bounce up and try it again.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This is a kid who doesn't want to wait for her teeth to fall out naturally. As soon as they're loose, she's trying to pull them out of her head. And she won't even let the tooth fairy take her teeth. She wants to make jewelry out of them. She's perfectly weird and brave in all the best ways.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So for her to shake and cry only with me is devastating. But also-- and I'm not proud of this-- a big part of me is like, girl, nobody's dying here. Suck it up.

segments.speaker: Avalon
segments.text: It hurts.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: Baby, I'm sorry. I have to get it.

segments.speaker: Avalon
segments.text: You already did.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: I didn't.

segments.speaker: Avalon
segments.text: Will it hurt always?

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: Probably, baby. Sometimes the things that we need are not comfortable.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Hold up. Did I just actually say that? I'm not even sure I believe it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: You know that moment when you open your mouth to say something and out comes your mother? This is one of the few times I heard that in my life, and it really stuck with me. My mom was the Black female dean of a military college. She taught me that sometimes in life, there are things like hair that you just have to tough out.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: In so much of my parenting, I've tried to be a little different, do it my way. I don't know if I totally believe that Black kids should just have to tough it out when they're in pain. I also don't want to be a parent that teaches their Black kid that everything in life should feel like a lukewarm bath.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When it comes to Avalon's hair, I feel so conflicted, like my two parenting styles are at war. And when I heard myself say, sometimes the things we need are not comfortable, I felt like I had to talk to my mom about it. I needed her to back me up on this. So I called her, Miss Martha Mathis herself.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I walked her through what had been going on with Avalon, the battle with her hair every day right before school. And I asked her, this is just the way it is, right, to which she said--

segments.speaker: Martha Mathis
segments.text: No. I think I've found that's what you want to avoid. Because at some point, if you're rushing and you're trying to do our hair, then it's going to hurt. If it's going to sit up there for days without anybody doing anything, then you're going to get what you get.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: My mom saying pain was something that you should or even could avoid was wild to me. She did my hair up so tightly I got migraines at school.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: Mama, do you remember one time when you were doing my hair, and you were doing it and doing it, and I was like, ow, ow! And I was eating breakfast at the breakfast table, and then I threw up?

segments.speaker: Martha Mathis
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: You don't remember that?

segments.speaker: Martha Mathis
segments.text: I don't, but that doesn't mean it didn't happen. It just means I don't remember it.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Martha Mathis
segments.text: Then what did we do?

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: Oh, you went and grabbed the trash can, just in case I had to again. But yeah, I just remember it hurting a lot.

segments.speaker: Martha Mathis
segments.text: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: My mom once described my parenting style as permissive. Sometimes I feel like I have to be firmer when she's around so she'll be proud of me, or something like that. So I couldn't quite wrap my head around what I was hearing.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: I'm kind of surprised to hear you say that, no, it doesn't have to hurt. I feel like you're a tough cookie, Mama.

segments.speaker: Martha Mathis
segments.text: I am.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: Yeah. And I feel like you raised me to be one. And I can feel that lesson starting as early as my hair, just as I can feel like I'm doing that with Avalon. Do you think that I should be making her tough for the world? Like the way I'm talking about hair is a gateway into, like, toughen up. Do you think that--

segments.speaker: Martha Mathis
segments.text: No. I wouldn't use hair as a gateway to toughen up because it has too many other racist and sexist implications.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: Did you want me to toughen up in those moments when I was crying and like, ouch, this hurts?

segments.speaker: Martha Mathis
segments.text: No, no. It hurt. No. Why would you-- no.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: You didn't want me to toughen up and just be like, we got to get used to this because we're on a schedule. We got places to go.

segments.speaker: Martha Mathis
segments.text: Well, it was going to happen whether you were tough or not. And at six-- I'll use Avalon's age-- she's as tough as she's going to be right now. And she can't be any tougher. I think she's the toughest little girl I know. So no, I would not have equated doing your hair with tough or not. I always felt bad that for those 10, 15, how many ever minutes it was, that that's how you were starting your day.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: I didn't know that she'd had any feelings about our mornings. My mother told me it was the same for her when she was young. She sat between her mother's knees, and out came the hot combs, the hair grease, the brushes, the pain, which she likes to remind me was far worse than mine, as I remind my daughter, and we copy and paste. But instead of giving me the validation I wanted and letting me know that the way she'd done my hair is really the only way, my mom gave me some advice I really wasn't looking for.

segments.speaker: Martha Mathis
segments.text: Give her some of her own hair.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: Oh, to take care of? Yes, I've tried this. We've tried this, yes.

segments.speaker: Martha Mathis
segments.text: Oh, you have?

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: Oh, yeah. We've tried-- it's do-your-own-hair day.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Do-your-own-hair day in my house means we give Avalon a brush and some bows, and 15 minutes later, absolutely nothing has happened. But it turned out that wasn't what my mother was suggesting.

segments.speaker: Martha Mathis
segments.text: No, I mean, have her do her own kitchen.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: Well.

segments.speaker: Martha Mathis
segments.text: She'll be gentle with herself.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: If she does her own hair at this age, Mama, she's avoiding her kitchen altogether.

segments.speaker: Martha Mathis
segments.text: What? OK. So it looks like-- I don't know-- a rat's nest. Nobody's going to see it.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Martha Mathis
segments.text: And if you remind her now, get in there, because you don't want me in there. Would you remind her of that? It's going to be your hand or mine.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Martha Mathis
segments.text: I think if you give her something that she owns and if it's just this little bit back there, my goodness, let her have it. What would happen if you parted that off, though, seriously?

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: I'm hearing you. I just don't-- I'm like-- when you're saying, why don't you try this, why don't you try giving Avalon a little section for herself, why didn't you try that with me?

segments.speaker: Martha Mathis
segments.text: Because no one told me that. That's how messages are passed on. The women my age, they were not brought up to even have these kind of conversations. And I don't even know if I had them in my brain, I mean, back then. But I'm saying for you, I would think you do have options. When you know better, you do better.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: The next time I did Avalon's hair, I let her do some of it.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: You ready to get the back just a little bit right here? Good job. Back here. Look at that. Why are you smiling? Whenever Mama's doing it, you're crying.

segments.speaker: Avalon
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: What's it feel like to do your own hair?

segments.speaker: Avalon
segments.text: Soft.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: It feels soft, huh?

segments.speaker: Avalon
segments.text: It doesn't feel hard like a rock. But when Mama does it, it feels hard like a rock.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: Your hair feels hard like a rock, or my brushing feels hard like a rock?

segments.speaker: Avalon
segments.text: The brushing feels hard like a rock.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: Does this part hurt?

segments.speaker: Avalon
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: Oh, good. I don't think I've ever seen your kitchen look so good. Should we show Papa?

segments.speaker: Avalon
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: Papa Bear! Do you want to tell him? Want to tell him?

segments.speaker: Avalon
segments.text: Look at my kitchen.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: [GASPS] Wow.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: What about your kitchen?

segments.speaker: Avalon
segments.text: I did it.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: You did it?

segments.speaker: Avalon
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Good job, baby.

segments.speaker: Myra Flynn
segments.text: As a parent, you're always looking for your failures. There are so many ways to fall short. But every once in a while, if you're lucky, the evidence is clear. You did something really good for your kid. And with my mom's help, I was able to change this one thing in the wheel of my own motherhood, and maybe one day, Avalon's. I want her to know what my mother knew and her mother before her, that when you're doing your hair some parts need someone else's hands, and some parts we can learn to hold ourselves.
